comments.body:
## Stage 1 dossier — and THREE corrections to what I originally filed on this ticket

Running the hypothesis-driven protocol (/rebar-debug) to prove or refute the stated mechanism.
Stage 1 gathering has already falsified parts of my own filing. Correcting them here rather than
letting the wrong narrative stand while the investigation runs.

### CORRECTION 1 — "climbing steadily all afternoon then collapsed" is WRONG

There was a LULL immediately before onset. Root VolumeReadOps (5-min sums, PDT):

```
13:50 225,696 | 13:55 303,222 | 14:00 377,530
14:05 122,622 | 14:10 108,782 | 14:15  82,165 | 14:20  64,397 | 14:25   8,333   <- near IDLE
14:30 448,361 | 14:35 755,609 | 14:40 765,839 | 14:45 774,668 | 14:50 775,351
14:55 768,166 | 15:00 753,944 | 15:05 420,072 (stop/start) | 15:10 159,499
```

At 14:25 the root volume was doing 8,333 reads — essentially idle. **The storm erupted out of a
QUIET period, not a crescendo.** That materially weakens "gradually accumulating load caused
gradual exhaustion", which is the story I told.

### CORRECTION 2 — the memory trajectory argues AGAINST the memory-exhaustion mechanism

`rebar/host:mem_available_percent` (PDT):

```
13:02 34 | 13:08 28 | 13:14 30 | 13:19 31 | 13:25 33 | 13:31 29 | 13:40 26 | 13:47 27
13:52 44 | 13:58 39 | 14:04 36 | 14:07 57 | 14:12 39 | 14:18 38 | 14:22 45 | 14:28 46
```

Memory was **TIGHTEST (26-29%) around 13:31-13:47 and nothing happened.** It then RECOVERED, and
stood at **46% — near the afternoon's best — at the moment the incident began.** Under a
memory-exhaustion mechanism the trajectory should be the opposite.

CAVEAT held honestly: Linux `MemAvailable` counts reclaimable page cache, so it can flatter a
thrashing box. That keeps H1 alive rather than dead. But the DIRECTION is wrong, and "improving
into the incident" is not what the hypothesis predicts.

### CORRECTION 3 — I had the causal ORDER backwards

All `rebar/host` publishing stopped at ~14:26-14:28. The read storm begins in the 14:30-14:35
bucket. **The publisher died BEFORE the storm, by 2-4 minutes** — so the storm cannot be what
killed it. Any surviving explanation must account for that ordering.

### Additional discriminating evidence gathered

- **The volume is gp3 provisioned at 3,000 IOPS.** Sustained ~2,580 read IOPS is ~86% of that,
  held flat within ~3% for 30 minutes. `VolumeQueueLength` went 0.02-1.5 -> **pinned 2.68-2.79**;
  `VolumeTotalReadTime` avg ~8-60 -> **pinned ~160-167**. Genuine saturation, not a reporting
  artifact.
- **Writes stayed near ZERO throughout** (215-550), against bursts of 126,156 at 14:00 and 87,600
  at the reboot. Read-only saturation. Notable because swap activity would appear as writes.
- **The DATA volume went nearly IDLE** while root saturated: 224,488 at 14:20 collapsing to
  2,604 / 5,200 / 2,774 / 4,265 / 2,522 / 1,942. **The storm was ROOT-ONLY** — consistent with
  Gerrit being unable to serve rather than Gerrit doing heavy work.

### What any surviving hypothesis must explain

1. Onset from a near-idle root volume at ~14:30.
2. The publisher dying 2-4 minutes BEFORE the storm.
3. Reads saturating while writes stay near zero.
4. The data volume going idle.
5. EC2 system AND instance status checks staying `ok` throughout.
6. Memory availability being near its afternoon best at onset.

### Status

Stage 2 (hypothesis generation with discriminating experiments) is running. **No root cause is
confirmed.** The mechanism recorded in this ticket's description remains INFERRED and is now
partly contradicted; treat it as a live hypothesis under test, not as the finding. I will post
the confirmed account, or an honest failure to confirm, when Phase 1 exits.

Experiments will run in a sandbox VM or against retained CloudWatch data. **Production will not
be used for reproduction** — the host is live and serving.

comments.body:
# CONFIRMED ROOT CAUSE — Phase 1 complete (/rebar-debug protocol)

Two mechanisms, one incident. H1 supplies the ignition; H2 supplies the latch and the 41 minutes.
H1 alone cannot explain why it never recovered.

## H2 (SUSTAINER, experimentally confirmed) — 12 unbounded whole-journal scans on a unit that can never be killed

`infra/scripts/observability.sh` re-scans the ENTIRE retained journal 12 times per run — no
`--since`, no `--lines`, no `timeout`:
`:760`, `:788` (review-bot container), `:816` (autodeploy unit), `:976` (gerrit container), plus
**8 unconditional** `publish_autodeploy_marker_delta` calls (`:902,904,910,914,922,935,940,942`)
each running its own scan at `:883`. All 8 verified straight-line, not conditional. (My original
filing said 11; it is 12.)

Two unit properties turn an expensive probe into a LATCH — confirmed empirically on real systemd 255:

1. `infra/scripts/install-observability.sh:20-27` declares `Type=oneshot` with **no
   `TimeoutStartSec`**. systemd reports `TimeoutStartUSec=infinity` for such a unit even though
   `DefaultTimeoutStartUSec=1min 30s`. A run that overruns hangs FOREVER; nothing kills it.
2. `:31` sets `OnUnitActiveSec=5min`, computed from the last COMPLETED activation. A built
   equivalent (5 s period, hanging ExecStart) after 25 s showed:
   `ActiveState=activating SubState=start` — exactly ONE run ever started — and
   **`NextElapseUSecMonotonic=infinity`**. A hung run does not delay the timer; it **deletes its
   next elapse.** Permanent silence, no self-recovery short of a reboot.

`infra/terraform/user_data.sh` sets NO journald tuning, so `SystemMaxUse` is the systemd default
`min(10% of 60 GiB, 4 GiB)` = **4 GiB on the root volume**.

### Measured (colima Ubuntu 24.04 aarch64, cgroup v2 io.max throttled to gp3's 3,000 IOPS / 125 MB/s, read_ahead_kb=16)

| Corpus | Conditions | Wall | vs 300s | Read | IOPS | MB/s |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0.49 GB | cold once, native NVMe | 11.8 s | 4% | 0.48 GB | 1,425 | 172 |
| 1.9 GB | cold once, native | 128.8 s | 43% | 1.78 GB | 758 | 96 |
| **1.86 GB** | **cold, gp3-throttled** | **407.5 s** | **136%** | **19.76 GB** | **2,985** | **48.2** |

Corpus was REAL journald data via `systemd-journal-remote` — genuine `.journal` files, indexed
`CONTAINER_NAME=`, real `_SYSTEMD_UNIT=`, 45 rotated files, 2.88M entries. Production matchers ran
verbatim and returned correct non-zero counts (23,060 / 6,410 / 17,427), so the field index was
genuinely exercised.

**Threshold: the 300 s period is exhausted at ~1.37 GB of retained journal** — far below the 4 GiB
cap the deployment actually configures. Projected to 4 GiB (linearity well-supported; read volume
tracked corpus at 12.1x and 12.0x across two sizes): **~940 s per run, a 3.1x overrun, ~45.6 GB
read.**

### CONTROL — unboundedness is the operative variable

Same journal, same throttle, both cold: unbounded **33,936 ms** vs `-n 5000` **798 ms** — **42.5x**.
Each scan read ~1.65 GB of the 1.86 GB corpus: the field index does NOT reduce bytes read,
`journalctl` still traverses every journal file. Twelve BOUNDED scans would cost ~10 s.

## H1 (TRIGGER, evidenced) — a page-cache eviction, not memory exhaustion

`container_memory_rss_bytes` (anon RSS; page cache cannot contaminate it) shows mcp swinging
0.52 -> 2.65 -> 1.05 -> 2.83 -> 3.15 -> 2.30 -> **3.02 GB at 14:25**, against gerrit steady at 1.00
and review-bot falling to 0.10. Total anon ~4.16 GB of 8 GiB — NOT exhaustion.

The 14:05-14:25 lull is the tell: 8,333 reads/5 min = **~28 IOPS** means the working set was
entirely in page cache and the probe was completing cheaply. One transient allocation at ~14:26
evicted it. From then every scan went cold, the run overran, the disk pinned, and nothing could
re-warm the cache.

## How this explains ALL SIX constraints

1. **Onset from a near-idle volume** — cache was warm (28 IOPS); eviction made the next scans cold.
2. **Publisher died 2-4 min BEFORE the storm** — it is ONE event, not two. The script publishes
   cheap metrics EARLY and does the journal work LATE. The publisher did not die and get followed
   by a storm; **the publisher entered the storm**, and by the latch above could never leave.
3. **Reads saturate, writes near zero** — journal scanning is read-only.
4. **Data volume went idle** — the only data-volume read (`:669` REPL_LOG grep) sits BEFORE the
   journal scans, so a run stuck later shows data reads once then nothing. Observed exactly:
   224,488 -> 84,772 -> 62,887 -> ~2,600.
5. **EC2 checks stayed ok** — they test hypervisor and network reachability, not app responsiveness.
6. **Memory near its afternoon best at onset** — `MemAvailable` counts reclaimable page cache
   (documented at `observability.sh:506-509`), so it reads healthy under cache thrash; and H1 is
   the trigger, not the sustainer.

## Corrections to earlier claims on this ticket

- **12 scans, not 11.**
- **"~3 concurrent synchronous readers" was over-read.** Little's law explains the queue depth on
  device latency alone: `2,585 IOPS x 1.035 ms = 2.68` exactly. It is ONE sequential scanner with
  readahead on a ~1 ms network-attached device. Local NVMe serves the identical stream at ~30 us
  (`2,985 x 0.03 ms = 0.09`).
- **EBS-side degradation is REFUTED** — 1.035 ms/op at that rate is a healthy gp3 volume.

## Defect legitimacy: DEFECT, against the script's OWN documented contract

`observability.sh:291-292` bounds its docker calls and states the rule: `DOCKER_DU_TIMEOUT=120`,
`DOCKER_DF_TIMEOUT=20`, commented *"Both docker calls are BOUNDED, the §2d rule: a wedged daemon
under disk pressure must not hold the 5-minute timer open"*, restated at `:545-551`. **The 12
journalctl scans violate the script's own §2d rule**, and the unit violates it again by omitting
`TimeoutStartSec` on a `Type=oneshot`. `AGENTS.md` §"Bound background helpers at spawn" mandates
the same.

Secondly the probe's stated design contract is *"a probe that could not measure publishes NOTHING
rather than a plausible 0"* and *"its ABSENCE means the probe/timer/host is dead"* (`:280`, `:487`).
A probe that can silence itself permanently by hanging **inverts its own heartbeat semantics** —
absence came to mean "the probe is stuck", not "the host is dead", while reading identically.

## Sandbox fidelity, stated honestly

Not EBS (local NVMe ~30 us vs ~1 ms; compensated with io.max + 16 KiB readahead so the IOPS
ceiling binds — hence the queue-depth divergence, which Little's law fully explains). Corpus was
1.86 GB not 4 GiB (`systemd-journal-remote` self-vacuums at the same 10%-of-fs rule — which
independently corroborates the 4 GiB arithmetic); the 4 GiB figures are labelled projections, and
this cuts in the confirming direction since 1.86 GB ALREADY overran by 36%. Smaller VM (2 vCPU /
3.9 GB): notably, even unthrottled and fully cached, 1.9 GB took 128.8 s — a CPU/parse floor of
~65 s/GB that alone reaches ~280 s at 4 GiB, brushing the period before any I/O contention. The
30-minute plateau was not reproduced directly; it follows from the latch, which was confirmed
separately on real systemd.

Production was never touched.

## Status

Root cause CONFIRMED. Defect attribution (`caused_by`) in progress; repair not yet started.

compiled_state.description:
## The incident

2026-09-04, ~21:28-22:09 UTC (41 minutes). The Gerrit host stopped serving entirely: HTTP 000
connection timeouts on every endpoint, all `rebar/host` metric publishing ceased. Ten alarms fired
correctly. Recovered by an operator-authorised stop/start.

## Root cause: root-volume EBS IOPS SATURATION, not space exhaustion

Root-volume `VolumeReadOps` (5-minute sums, PDT):

```
14:22    57,451     normal
14:27    31,251     normal  (last metrics published 14:26)
14:32   716,017     <- onset, ~25x jump
14:37   760,455
14:42   780,422
14:47   769,645     <- pinned FLAT for 30 minutes
14:52   776,284
14:57   765,705
15:02   740,235
15:07   274,858     <- stop/start
```

Four minutes after the publisher died, root reads jumped ~25x and **pinned dead flat at roughly
2,500 IOPS** for the entire outage. A flat ceiling is saturation against a device limit, not
organic load.

This is the signature of **memory exhaustion driving page-cache thrashing**: the kernel evicts
cache under pressure, then continuously re-reads executable pages from disk, saturating root EBS
and starving userspace. It explains every observed symptom together — nothing accepted connections
on 443, the metrics publisher stopped, and EC2 status checks nonetheless stayed `ok`, because
those test the hypervisor and network reachability rather than application responsiveness.

Reads were also **climbing steadily all afternoon** — ~60k at 11:12 PDT to ~440k by 13:37 — before
the collapse, consistent with accumulating concurrent load rather than a sudden event.

## THE DISTINCTION THAT MATTERS: this is not what epic 6202 bounds

**Root disk was only 47% FULL at the time.** The `rebar-root-disk-pressure` alarm threshold is 85%
and was nowhere near tripping on space.

Epic 6202 ("Bounded disk-ceiling architecture") bounds disk SPACE — overlay2, BuildKit cache,
journald, /var/tmp, container layers, and a dedicated scratch volume. **None of that would have
prevented this outage**, and none of it detects this condition. A host can sit at 40% full and be
completely unavailable because its root volume is IOPS-saturated.

Ticket `cyclopean-bloodshot-hoatzin` covers root disk FILLING (the 2026-09-02 incident, 97% full).
This is a different failure mode with the same visible symptom, which is exactly why it is filed
separately rather than as a comment there — conflating them would let "we bounded disk" read as
"we fixed the host going offline".

## Contributing load, stated honestly

The concurrent load that afternoon was substantially agent-driven: up to five subagents running in
parallel, several executing plan-review gates through the on-box MCP server, alongside full local
test suites. A prior audit had already measured ~9.6 GB of demand against an 8 GiB host when
reviews stack, with `deploy_deferrals` at 69/24h as contention evidence, and `mem_available_percent`
is **measurement-only with no alarm** (tracked on `witted-invisible-roan`).

So the trigger is very likely self-inflicted concurrency. That does not make it a non-bug: a host
that becomes completely unavailable under load it is asked to accept, with no admission control on
the dimension that saturates and no alarm on it, is a real defect. Story S6 added gate admission
bounded by CONCURRENCY COUNT; nothing bounds or observes memory or IOPS.

## Evidence that is permanently gone

`aws ec2 get-console-output` returned data timestamped two days stale during the incident, and
after the stop/start returns EMPTY — the buffer was wiped. There is no direct kernel OOM-kill
record and there never can be for this incident. See `fab-dismal-haddock`.

So the mechanism above is **strongly evidenced but not proven**: the IOPS signature is measured,
the memory-exhaustion explanation for it is inference.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] AC1 - Root-volume IOPS saturation is DETECTED. An alarm exists on the dimension that actually
      saturated, so this condition pages rather than being reconstructed afterwards from EBS
      metrics. State the threshold and why.
- [ ] AC2 - Memory pressure is detected before it cascades. `mem_available_percent` is currently
      measurement-only. Coordinate with `witted-invisible-roan` rather than duplicating its work.
- [ ] AC3 - Admission control considers the resource that actually exhausts. S6 bounds concurrent
      gates by COUNT; demonstrate the chosen bound holds when concurrent work is heterogeneous
      (a plan review, a full suite, and a build are not interchangeable units).
- [ ] AC4 - Documented in the tree: bounding disk SPACE does not bound disk IOPS, and epic 6202
      does not address this failure mode. A future reader must not infer protection that does not
      exist.
- [ ] AC5 - Defect-seeded: the detection from AC1 fires against tonight's recorded EBS series
      (~2,500 IOPS flat for 30 minutes). A detector that would not have caught this incident has
      not been shown to work.
compiled_state.title: Gerrit went fully offline for 41 minutes from root-volume EBS IOPS saturation at only 47% disk full: epic 6202 bounds disk SPACE and would not have prevented or detected it
